newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall in disappointment over IBM.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall in disappointment over IBM.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell Wednesday on disappointment over International Business Machines Corp.'s earnings, but the Nasdaq Composite index hit another record high on upbeat results from other technology companies.
Bonds fell in thin trading as investors took profits before Thursday's five-year Treasury note auction.
The dollar rose against major currencies after Japanese and French officials said the Group of Seven industrialised nations backed the U.S. position favouring a strong dollar.

The 30-stock Dow Jones industrial average ended down 33.87 points at 6,850.03, and virtually all of the loss stemmed from IBM, which tumbled $10.375 to $157.625. The drop in the index snapped a four-session string of record closes.
The Nasdaq gained 11.09 points to 1,388.06, beating Tuesday's record close of 1,376.97. The Standard & Poor's 500 and NYSE Composite indexes also set new highs.
Beyond the drop in IBM, the overall market's performance was mixed.

But the spotlight was fixed squarely on Big Blue, the computer giant whose results prompted many Wall Street analysts to trim their earnings estimates, indicating earlier expectations for the company had run ahead of reality.
"Rather than easily achieve Street estimates, IBM appeared to be huffing and puffing," said Steve Milunovich, an analyst at investment bank Morgan Stanley.

In the bond market, the price of the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond dropped 19/32 point, or $5.94 on a $1,000 bond, sending its yield up to 6.83 percent from Tuesday's close of 6.79 percent. The bond's price and yield move in opposite directions.

The dollar rose to 119.03 Japanese yen from 117.91 yen Tuesday, and to 1.6421 German marks from 1.6296 marks. It also set a 32-month high of 1.4360 Swiss francs, before settling at 1.4295, up from 1.4180 Swiss francs Tuesday.

The dollar was boosted by comments by Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and Bank of France Gov. Jean-Claude Trichet, who said the G7 nations supported U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's preference for a strong dollar.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, heating oil prices went up on expectations the weekly oil inventory data would show a decline in stocks following the chilly weather. February heating oil rose 0.86 cent to 66.89 cents a gallon.

In the data released by the American Petroleum Institute after trading closed, stocks of distillates, which include heating oil and diesel, fell 2.95 million barrels to 122.50 million in the week ended Jan. 17, in line with analyst expectations for a drop of 3 million barrels.
February gasoline ended up 0.78 cent to 68.22 cents a gallon, and March crude oil 2 cents higher at $24.24 a barrel.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 rose 23.6 points to 4,219.1, surpassing the previous record of 4,207.7 set on Jan. 17. In Tokyo, the key Nikkei average of 225 leading shares closed up 655.72 points at 18,013.88.
